title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
purpose: It compiles the rulings, fatwa-answers and esoteric interpretations governing the Friday prayer and the prayers of the two festivals, joining legal detail to symbolic (batini) exegesis.

points.text: A cited question-and-answer collection, arranged by the chapters of Daaim al-Islam, rules that Friday prayer may be established in two congregational mosques only if three miles or more separate them — and the answer extends this: if the distance is less than three miles, Friday is established in only one of them, whether the mosques belong to one city or two.

Against al-Muayyad's sermon wording that condemns abandoning Friday prayer 'under a just imam or an unjust one', the answer distinguishes two senses: praying behind the people of injustice is impermissible except under taqiyya (dissimulation), whereas 'the unjust' in the sermon means an appointed summoner in whom transgression has appeared, behind whom prayer remains obligatory while the people refer the matter to the holder of authority.

Al-Baqir Muhammad ibn Ali is reported as instructing that prayer behind a nasib or a haruri not be counted, the leader being treated as a mere pillar of the mosque while one recites for oneself as if praying alone.

Al-Husayn ibn Ali is reported to have let Muawiya's governor lead the prayer over al-Hasan, saying 'were it not for the practice I would not have put you forward', which the text glosses as the People of the House's practice of dissimulation, summed up in an Imam's saying that 'dissimulation is my religion and the religion of my fathers'.

Mukhtasar al-Musannaf supplies the practical rules of Friday: prayer behind the Imam of the Muslims surpasses prayer behind his deputies; the binding call is the one given before the seated preacher; a broken purity lets the Imam withdraw, wash, and either repeat the sermon or simply pray; a seated sermon suffices for illness; and omitting the sitting between the two sermons is disliked but not grounds for repetition.

The number of cycles depends on when the congregation disperses: if all but one man leave after the sermon the Imam prays four, if they leave after one completed cycle he prays Friday as two, and if they leave before he bows he restarts as the four-cycle noon prayer.

Tawil al-Shariah states that the sermon precedes the two-cycle Friday prayer, is divided in two by a sitting, is distinguished from ordinary noon prayer by the raised voice, and that the call to stand comes after the sermon; it also makes the summoner's assembly parallel to the Friday congregation, so that silence and attentive listening become obligatory once the preacher faces the people.

Tawil al-Shariah forbids the respondent to 'give suck' unless appointed to it by his summoner, and forbids him to press proposals or demand branches of knowledge from the summoner, who 'knows better how to raise his children'.

Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl's Hidden Epistle reads Friday esoterically: it points to Muhammad, gate of the Garden, who has an outward summons to the zahir of his law and an inward summons to its interpretation; the two cycles replace four because the sermon substitutes for two, and the sitting within the sermon is the separation between the upper and lower lights with which the Qaim rises.

The section reports that tashriq, said to be incumbent only in a congregational city, means the prayer of the two festivals — so named because it is prayed at sunrise and its performer is called al-mushriq — and that the twenty-three magnifications from Arafah to the last day of tashriq are a likeness of the summons of the five speakers of firm resolve corresponding to the five prayers, the ten spiritual and ten bodily ranks, and the speaker of the cycle, his executor, and the Imam of the age.

The festival prayer has neither call to prayer nor call to stand, requires a congregation of five including the Imam like Friday, is obligatory where someone establishes it, and is not prayed in congregation at Mina — where, per al-Numan's Tawil al-Daaim and Idris ibn Hasan, each prays it alone.

The Hidden Epistle derives fitr from the sense of splitting open, appearing and beginning — as earth, tree and camel's tooth 'break forth' — so that, fasting being silence and concealment as in Maryam's vow of a fast of silence, the breaking of the fast is the day the veiled command and hidden secrets are manifested; and the festival-of-sacrifice sermon uniquely begins with four magnifications rather than praise, signalling that the command appears otherwise than in past cycles.
